t: Count Substrings Rearrangeable to Contain word2: Minimal-Window Two Pointers
o: "Can be rearranged to have word2 as a prefix" simply means the substring contains at least count[c] copies of each character c of word2 — rearrangement is free, so only multiset containment matters. Validity is monotone: extending a valid substring to the left keeps it valid. Hence for each right endpoint r there is a minimal valid left boundary l(r), non-decreasing in r, and the number of valid substrings ending at r is l(r)+1 (starts 0..l(r)). Example 2: once a window holds a,b,c, every longer window ending at r also qualifies.
k: Validity = per-character counts dominate word2's counts; no ordering constraint exists.
Two pointers: grow r, shrink l while the window stays valid; after shrinking, every start ≤ l gives a valid substring ending at r.
Shrink only while removal keeps validity (stop when word1[l] is 'critical'), giving amortized O(n) despite the 1e6 length.

a.n: Approach 1: Sliding Window with Deficit Counter
a.i: Maintain counts of word2 characters inside the window and a `missing` counter of character types still below their requirement. When missing hits 0 the window is valid; advance l while the leftmost character is surplus (its count exceeds the requirement), stopping just before validity would break. Add l+1 valid substrings per r.
s: Compute need[26] from word2 and missing = number of distinct chars in word2.
For each r, increment count[word1[r]]; if it reaches need, decrement missing.
While missing == 0: if count[word1[l]] would drop below need, stop; else decrement and l++.
If valid, add l+1 to the answer.
a.t: O(|word1| + |word2|) — each pointer advances at most |word1| times; meets the strict linear requirement

w: This two-pointer counting pattern (add l+1 per right end) is the canonical answer; a per-character-prefix-sum or binary-search approach also works in O(26n) but risks the tight memory limit. Pitfalls: counting substrings of length < |word2| (they can never qualify — the window logic handles this automatically), off-by-one on `l+1` versus `l`, and using 32-bit accumulators (answer can exceed 2^31). Follow-ups: count substrings containing word2 as a *contiguous* substring (classic minimum-window sliding count), or handle wildcards.
